paper_title: MFVSR: A Multi-Style and Fine-Grained Benchmark for Video Subtitle Removal

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video subtitle removal (VSR) is an important video restoration task, yet existing evaluation remains limited by low-resolution datasets, fragmented test sets, and generic video-inpainting protocols that fail to adequately capture localized restoration errors, unintended modifications, temporal instability, and incomplete outputs. In this paper, we introduce MFVSR, a large-scale multi-style benchmark for fine-grained and reliability-aware video subtitle removal evaluation. MFVSR distinguishes itself through three key features: (1) Large-scale and diverse data, comprising 3,000 paired videos from Real-HQ, Real-LQ, and AI-Generated sources, with an auxiliary set of 953 in-the-wild real videos for real-world coverage analysis; (2) Controlled subtitle diversity, spanning 16 languages and four factors covering spatial layout, temporal behavior, visual style, and language mode; (3) Fine-grained evaluation, introducing an information-conditioned, spatially decoupled protocol that separates blind from mask-guided removal and measures Restoration Fidelity, Preservation Fidelity, Temporal Fidelity, coverage, and failures. Experiments on six representative methods reveal substantial discrepancies between local restoration, outside-region preservation, temporal consistency, and full-set reliability that are obscured by conventional full-frame metrics. MFVSR therefore provides a more comprehensive and diagnostic foundation for evaluating and advancing video subtitle removal methods.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video Subtitle Removal (VSR) aims to remove burned-in subtitles while reconstructing the occluded background and preserving the original visual content (Kim et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021). Although closely related to video inpainting and scene text removal (Zhang et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), VSR presents distinct combination of challenges: subtitle regions must be accurately localized, covered scene content must be faithfully restored, unaffected regions should remain unchanged, and the reconstructed video must remain temporally consistent across frames. These challenges are further complicated by variations in subtitle layout, visual style, language, resolution, and temporal behavior. Consequently, comprehensive evaluation of existing methods is essential for understanding their capabilities and limitations and for supporting reliable progress in VSR. However, existing public resources remain insufficient for such systematic VSR evaluation, presenting three core limitations: (L1) Fragmented benchmark coverage. ChaLearn (ChaLearn Looking at People, 2018; Kim et al., 2019) is limited to short 128 128 clips, while recent methods such as SEDiT (Hui & Bai, 2026) and CLEAR (He et al., 2026) rely on independently constructed paper-specific test sets. As result, current evaluations cover only narrow range of video sources, resolutions, and real-world content distributions, making broad and reproducible comparison difficult. (L2) Insufficiently structured subtitle variation. Existing test sets include diverse subtitle appearances, but these variations are rarely organized along explicit and independently controlled factors such as spatial layout, temporal behavior, visual style, and language. It spans 16 languages and four subtitle factors, and evaluates blind and mask-guided removal through five spatial views and three complementary dimensions: Restoration Fidelity, Preservation Fidelity, and Temporal Fidelity. to attribute performance differences to specific subtitle conditions or to conduct systematic stratified analysis. (L3) Generic Benchmarks Lack Subtitle-Specific Evaluation Design. Broader video-inpainting evaluation resources and benchmarks (Perazzi et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2019; Szeto & Corso, 2022; Wu et al., 2025; Miao et al., 2025) improve content diversity, motion coverage, temporal evaluation, and restoration diagnosis, but are not designed around multilingual subtitle structure, the information asymmetry between blind localization and mask-guided restoration, or spatially decoupled diagnosis with explicit coverage and failure accounting. The core gap is therefore not merely lack of data, but the absence of unified benchmark that combines high-resolution paired supervision, controlled subtitle diversity, complementary real-world subtitle coverage, and information-conditioned, spatially decoupled evaluation. To directly address these limitations, we propose MFVSR, Multi-style and Fine-grained benchmark for Video Subtitle Removal, as shown in Figure 1. MFVSR is built around three key contributions: (1) Large-scale and diverse data. MFVSR contains 3,000 resolution-diverse paired videos, balanced equally across the Real-HQ, Real-LQ, and AI-Generated source strata. Controlled subtitle rendering provides paired clean targets, pixel-level glyph masks, frame-level BBoxes, BBox-derived model-input masks, and rendering metadata, enabling fine-grained evaluation against known clean content. In addition, we curate an auxiliary set of 953 naturally subtitled in-the-wild real videos from Bilibili, Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Kuaishou, and YouTube to broaden coverage of real-world subtitle appearances and content distributions. (2) Controlled subtitle diversity. MFVSR covers 16 languages and factorizes subtitle rendering into four independently configurable factors: Spatial Layout, Temporal Behavior, Visual Style, and Language Mode, yielding 24 configuration cells. This controlled design facilitates standardized cross-method comparison and stratified analysis, without presupposing that any language or rendering factor is inherently more challenging. (3) Fine-grained evaluation. MFVSR separates blind subtitle removal from mask-guided removal. Predictions are evaluated using five spatial views and grouped into Restoration Fidelity, Preservation Fidelity, and Temporal Fidelity. It also jointly reports conditional quality, spatial and temporal coverage, partial outputs, and full-benchmark failures. We evaluate six representative subtitle-removal, video-inpainting, and object-removal methods under MFVSR. The results reveal distinct trade-offs across restoration, preservation, temporal fidelity, and reliability that conventional full-frame similarity does not capture. Held-out human comparisons provide stronger support for the spatial components than for the temporal component, and do not establish an advantage of SR-Q over conventional Overall metrics. sections.title: 2.1 MULTI-SOURCE COLLECTION AND BASE-VIDEO FILTERING
sections.content: Multi-source collection for MFVSR. To cover different content origins, resolutions, durations, scenes, and motion patterns, MFVSR contains 3,000 clean base videos from real and generated sources. We divide them into three equal strata. Real-HQ contains 1,000 real videos from OpenVidHD and Pexels (Nan et al., 2025; Pexels, 2026), with retained resolution at or above 1080p. RealLQ contains 1,000 real videos from Panda-70M and Pexels (Chen et al., 2024; Pexels, 2026), with retained resolution at or above 512p and below 1080p. AI-Generated contains 1,000 videos from the VBench-2.0 sampled-video release (Zheng et al., 2025) and the Rapidata Sora video-generation alignment dataset (Rapidata, 2025). Real-HQ and Real-LQ are resolution-based strata rather than perceptual-quality labels, and the three sources do not imply exhaustive content coverage. Automatic and manual filtering. We use automatic screening followed by manual verification. Automatic screening samples frames, checks decoding and basic validity, filters by resolution and preliminary clarity, and uses OCR to flag burned-in text, URLs, and other overlays. Manual verification removes videos with burned-in subtitles, salient watermarks, subtitle-like text overlays, static slideshows, cartoons, anime, or other content unsuitable for paired subtitle rendering. Small logos may remain if they are fixed in corner and cannot be confused with the rendered subtitles. Large, prominent, textual, or subtitle-region watermarks are excluded. The resulting clean videos enter the rendering pipeline in Figure 2. Additional asset-validation checks are described in Appendix B.1.

sections.content: Figure 3: Controlled subtitle-rendering taxonomy in MFVSR. The two-level ring summarizes four independently configurable factors: Spatial Layout, Temporal Behavior, Visual Style, and Language Mode and their major options, forming 24 configuration cells. Surrounding examples are color-coded by factor to illustrate finer-grained within-cell variations. Russian for Cyrillic; Arabic and Persian for right-to-left scripts; and Hindi and Thai for additional writing systems. These languages introduce different glyph structures, shaping rules, reading directions, and layout characteristics without assuming language-specific difficulty order. Fonts are divided into regular and style-oriented resources. Multi-level taxonomy combination rendering. MFVSR structures the taxonomy around the changing aspect of subtitle over its display interval, spanning four independently configurable axes. The four independently configurable factors form Spatial Layout Temporal Behavior Visual Style Language Mode, which yields 2 2 3 2 = 24 major configuration cells. And finer-grained subtypes add further within-cell variation, as shown in Figure 3. Spatial layout governs where subtitle appears and whether its coordinates change over time: fixed subtitles occupy one of five anchors with constant coordinates, whereas dynamic subtitles follow one of four trajectories, making position function of time. Temporal behavior captures how subtitle evolves between appearance and disappearance. Static subtitles remain unchanged while visible, whereas animated subtitles comprise nine subtypes that cover entrance transformations of whole blocks, reveals at the character level, and persistent perturbations. Spatial layout and temporal behavior are orthogonal and may occur together. For example, caption can translate from point to point (spatial, dynamic), while fade-in or typewriter effect alters its form without displacing it (temporal, animated). Therefore, we retain them as separate axes. Visual style determines how glyphs are rendered, ranging from plain (color variation only), to decorated (shadows, outlines, or background boxes for functional separation), to stylized (glow, gradients, neon, textures, or expressive fonts). Language mode sets how many languages appear simultaneously: monolingual subtitles contain single language, while bilingual subtitles pair two randomly selected languages, typically arranged in two lines, and configurations with more than two languages are excluded as uncommon in practice. The four axes combine to produce 24 major cells. While the factors are independent in configuration, their effects on removal difficulty may not be statistically independent. Therefore, potential mediators like subtitle area and line count are evaluated separately for each factor.

sections.title: 2.4 EXECUTION ROUTING
sections.content: MFVSR routes each integrated model through deterministic input preprocessing. All mask-guided methods start from the same canonical BBox-derived annotation. Model-specific operations, such as resizing, thresholding, and dilation when required, follow the evaluated inference configuration, and no routing or preprocessing step accesses the glyph mask, clean target, or manually adjusted samplespecific conditions. Blind removal takes only the subtitle-corrupted video as input, whereas maskguided removal additionally receives the canonical BBox-derived mask defined above. MFVSR therefore ranks the two families separately. Table 1 lists the resulting model interfaces.

The glyph mask is reserved for evaluation and is never exposed as model input. Because the two settings provide different information, they share targets and metrics but remain in separate result blocks. Every method retains its released resolution limit, precision, chunking, sampling, and deterministic mask adapter. Raw outputs are immutable: missing frames are neither copied nor padded, and metric is withheld when its spatial or temporal correspondence cannot be verified. All model interfaces are frozen in Table 6. Spatially decoupled evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 1, MFVSR evaluates five views: Overall, BBox, Subtitle, BBox-NG, and Outside. Subtitle, BBox-NG, and Outside partition each frame, BBox is the union of the first two, and Overall is the full frame. Because the glyph mask can omit shadows, outlines, glow, or subtitle boxes, BBox-NG mixes nearby background with non-core subtitle effects and is used only as local diagnostic. Boxed and Subtitle-box styles are analyzed separately because their affected support can extend beyond the text BBox. The five views are organized into three capabilities  (Table 3)  . Restoration Fidelity asks whether the subtitle core is replaced by the clean target; Preservation Fidelity asks whether content outside the operational BBox remains unchanged; and Temporal Fidelity asks whether the prediction introduces temporal error beyond the target motion. PSNR, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004), LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), DISTS (Ding et al., 2020), and RAFT (Teed & Deng, 2020) retain their released implementations and weights. Regional PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS change only the aggregation support; conditioned DISTS is explicitly controlled-input intervention, not an official dense DISTS variant. Overall metrics are retained for conventional full-frame compatibility rather than used as the primary evidence. Evaluation tracks and Audit300. We separate benchmark coverage from measurement density. Lite3000 provides broad spatial and temporal evaluation, whereas Audit300 adds more expensive structural and motion-compensated metrics on fixed 300-video subset. Sampling is frozen and shared across methods, and Audit300 is drawn from the common-evaluable pool using only dataset attributes, without access to model outputs, metric values, rankings, or human judgments. This provides controlled shared-ID set for detailed cross-method analysis. Selection details and composition are reported in Appendix B.2. Statistics and human alignment. Unless otherwise stated, quality results are video-level macro estimates with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, while delivery statistics use all scheduled videos. Cross-model comparisons use shared IDs and symmetric metric support, and model-native results are interpreted only conditionally. Reliability is reported separately from quality through complete, partial, and failed or missing outputs. Held-out human comparisons show stronger alignment for the spatial dimensions than for Temporal Fidelity, while the preregistered SR-Q summary shows no advantage over conventional Overall metrics and is retained only as secondary analysis. Full statistical and human-study procedures are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: 3.3 FINDINGS OF MFVSR
sections.content: We present five findings from MFVSR, with supporting analyses in Appendix C. Decoupled evaluation reveals quality trade-offs. Figure 5 and Table 4 show that Subtitle and Outside LPIPS disagree on five of ten mask-guided method pairs. For example, DiffuEraser has lower Subtitle LPIPS than ProPainter but higher Outside LPIPS. BBox TWE-Excess and BBox TC likewise disagree on six of ten pairs, highlighting non-interchangeable temporal evidence. Overall LPIPS follows Outside LPIPS more closely than Subtitle LPIPS. These descriptive comparisons include EffectErases verified-prefix results and support reporting Restoration, Preservation, and Temporal Fidelity separately rather than relying on full-frame scores alone. See Appendix C.2 for detailed comparisons. Subtitle removal performance varies across dataset dimensions and capabilities. Figure 6 shows that source, resolution, duration, and style complexity affect different capabilities in different ways. Real-HQ yields higher Subtitle and Outside LPIPS than AI-generated videos for all six methods, yet lower BBox TC for five, indicating that visually harder restoration does not necessarily imply greater temporal instability. Because source and resolution are coupled in Audit300, this contrast should be interpreted as property of the joint data strata rather than an isolated resolution effect. sections.title: 4 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we presented MFVSR, benchmark for systematic evaluation of video subtitle removal. MFVSR combines paired videos with controlled multilingual subtitle variations and an auxiliary collection of naturally subtitled videos. Its protocol distinguishes blind from mask-guided removal and separately evaluates restoration, preservation, temporal fidelity, and delivery coverage.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Experiments on six representative methods reveal quality trade-offs and gaps between conditional performance and complete-video delivery. The held-out human study shows stronger agreement for spatial than temporal components, leaving temporal perceptual validation open. We hope that MFVSR and its analyses support reproducible comparison and the development of more reliable video subtitle removal methods.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: MFVSR uses videos from OpenVidHD, Panda-70M, Pexels, VBench-2.0, and Rapidata, subtitle text from FLORES, and fonts from Google Fonts. These resources remain subject to their respective licenses and upstream restrictions. The auxiliary collection contains 953 naturally subtitled videos collected from Bilibili, Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Kuaishou, and YouTube using web crawler. No additional privacy screening or de-identification was applied to these videos. This collection has no clean targets and is excluded from paired quantitative evaluation. We plan to redistribute only assets for which redistribution is permitted, and otherwise provide permissible provenance information, annotations, and reconstruction instructions. We recruited students from relevant academic disciplines for the human evaluation. Participants were informed of the research purpose and agreed to participate before the study. The study interface used coded participant identifiers, and no additional identifying information was retained with the study responses. Participants compared subtitle-removal outputs using reference-based interface with concealed model identities. Human-evaluation results are reported only in aggregate in the manuscript.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Sections 2 and 3.1 describe the benchmark construction, model information boundaries, and evaluation design, while Appendix specifies spatial supports, metric regionalization, frozen frame and pair sampling, record reuse, aggregation, comparison sets, human evaluation, and fixed-budget validation. Across the six baselines, the retained inference logs cover total of 10,137.4 GPU-hours (422.4 GPU-days). Appendix details the logging coverage and method-specific timing boundaries. Subject to upstream licensing constraints, we plan to release the renderer, evaluation code, frozen identifiers, model configurations, analysis tables, and per-instance provenance records.

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Video Subtitle Removal. Video subtitle removal combines localization, completion, and temporal stabilization. The ChaLearn 2018 video-decaptioning task (ChaLearn Looking at People, 2018) provided paired corrupted and clean clips, while Kim et al. (2019) introduced blind encoderdecoder that aggregates neighboring frames with recurrent feedback without requiring an input mask. Recent diffusion-based methods revisit end-to-end mask-free removal at higher resolution. CLEAR (He et al., 2026) separates subtitle-prior extraction from generative refinement and performs mask-free inference, whereas SEDiT (Hui & Bai, 2026) formulates subtitle erasure as localized one-step video generation with chunk-wise streaming. These methods strengthen the case for dedicated task, but their paper-specific 400-sample evaluations do not provide shared, fine-grained protocol for diagnosing residual text, local reconstruction, distant modification, and failure coverage. The distinction between mask-free and mask-guided inference is methodological rather than cosmetic. blind method must infer both where and how to edit, whereas mask-guided method is given spatial side information. Combining both settings in one ranking conflates localization and restoration. MFVSR therefore uses the same paired targets and diagnostic views for both settings but reports them in separate leaderboard blocks. Video Inpainting and Object Removal. Most video-inpainting methods assume binary hole mask and focus on reconstructing spatially plausible and temporally coherent content. Flowguided methods such as E2FGVI (Li et al., 2022) propagate visible evidence across frames, while later transformerand diffusion-based approaches expand temporal context and generative capacity. ProPainter (Zhou et al., 2023) combines dual-domain propagation with mask-guided sparse video transformer, while DiffuEraser (Li et al., 2025) incorporates diffusion priors for masked video completion. Recent video-object-removal systems further target large objects and associated visual effects. MiniMax-Remover (Zi et al., 2026) reduces sampling cost through distilled removal model; OmnimatteZero (Samuel et al., 2025) uses pretrained video diffusion models to remove objects together with their footprints; and EffectErase (Fu et al., 2026) jointly learns removal and insertion to better handle shadows, reflections, and deformation. These methods are relevant baselines because the same canonical BBox-derived subtitle annotation can be deterministically adapted to their released interfaces. They are not subtitle localizers, however, and their mask-guided results are not presented as evidence of blind subtitle-removal ability. Diagnostic Benchmarking and Perceptual Evaluation. Generic video-inpainting evaluations commonly repurpose DAVIS (Perazzi et al., 2016) or YouTube-VOS (Xu et al., 2018) with synthetic masks, but aggregate scores reveal little about the conditions under which method fails. DEVIL (Szeto & Corso, 2022) addresses this limitation by labeling video and mask attributes

BVINet (Wu et al., 2025) defines blind video-inpainting setting and evaluates on 508 YouTubeVOS and 60 DAVIS clips with synthesized corruptions. These resources motivate controlled and diagnostic analysis, but their corruptions are not designed around multilingual subtitle typography, motion, animation, or language layout. MFVSR also follows the broader move from one-number evaluation toward dimension-specific evidence. VBench (Huang et al., 2024) decomposes video-generation quality into fine-grained dimensions and validates them against human preferences. For paired restoration, PSNR measures pixel-level distortion, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) measures local structural similarity, LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) provides learned perceptual distance, and DISTS (Ding et al., 2020) compares perceptual structure and texture. Temporal warping error (Lai et al., 2018) measures motion-compensated inconsistency. MFVSR retains the released metric definitions and weights where possible, changing only the spatial support or controlled input used for regional diagnosis. Because DISTS is an imagelevel score rather than dense map, its regional use is explicitly defined as conditioned DISTS in Appendix B, rather than presented as an official DISTS variant.

sections.content: C.5 EVALUABLE SCOPE AND CONDITIONAL QUALITY The final non-box primary pool has 2,499 videos; its six-model common intersection has 2,298. Table 13 gives each methods additional evaluable scope. These sets can overlap and are dominated by Real-LQ videos; all AI-generated primary-pool videos already lie in the common intersection. Figure 12 separates complete and partial outputs and distinguishes typical error from the upper tail. ProPainters added videos increase both median and tail Subtitle LPIPS. MiniMax-Remover instead has lower median but worse tail, which mean alone would conceal. For DiffuEraser and EffectErase, worse restoration on added videos coexists with lower BBox TC. For example, DiffuErasers median Subtitle LPIPS rises from 0.228 to 0.285, while median BBox TC falls from 0.0212 to 0.0187. MiniMax-Removers median Subtitle LPIPS falls from 0.253 to 0.219, while its 90th percentile rises from 0.558 to 0.671. These summaries pool complete and partial outputs with valid metrics. Lower temporal discrepancy or lower median can therefore conceal deterioration in another aspect of quality. The additional sets are selected by method evaluability and differ in composition. These shifts describe each methods expanded operating scope, not the effect of controlled increase in difficulty. Common-set results support shared-ID comparisons; native results reveal what those comparisons leave out and do not support cross-method rankings on different IDs. sections.title: E QUALITATIVE CASES AND DIAGNOSTIC INSIGHTS
sections.content: We retain five cases per diagnostic, selected by decreasing six-model range in Subtitle LPIPS, Outside LPIPS, or BBox TC (ties broken by video ID). Selection uses neither SR-Q nor human labels. Only unreadable assets, invalid common crops, or unavailable shared temporal support permit rejection. The gallery illustrates disagreements, not failure frequencies or an unbiased ranking. Case records retain IDs, frame indices, crops, and scores. Restoration comparisons use local crops; Preservation comparisons retain full-frame context. Temporal strips show three consecutive shared frames, read left to right. Views and aspect ratios are matched across methods. CLEAR is blind; the other methods receive BBox masks.
